question: to the Commission Kostas Papadakis (NI), Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

Three years after the crime of Tempi - a foregone conclusion - there is widespread demand for it not to be covered up, for criminal and political responsibility to be assigned, and for there never to be another ‘Tempi’. The causes are still here. The competent ERTMS coordinator of DG MOVE admits in a report that ‘only 10 % of the total TEN-T and 19 % of the EU railway fleet are equipped with ETCS’ and ‘the development of ERTMS is very slow’, while a goal is set of ‘reducing the cost of ERTMS on trains’. The EU and governments’ main criterion is ‘cost-benefit’, sacrificing security for the profits of business groups, while funding for military mobility is increased tenfold in the new MFF (2028-2034) and another 100 billion euro are announced - through the CEF - for the ‘military Schengen’. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that, three years after the inevitable crime of Tempi, train collisions are increasing throughout Europe, with dozens of deaths and injuries, as the railway liberalisation strategy and the EU and governments’ ‘costbenefit’ policy condemn the network to tragic shortages of personnel and a lack of modern security systems, infrastructure and maintenance, with painful consequences for the safety of passengers and workers?

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that, while the recruitment of personnel and the installation of modern security systems are at a standstill and a report by a Commission official recommends new ‘cost reductions’, even ‘on trains’, the Commission is promoting a tenfold increase in funding for military mobility and war preparation, involving the people of Europe in incalculable risks?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.5.2026) The Commission has no data that confirms a negative impact on safety of the rail market opening to competition. On the contrary safety indicators and safety performance data collected by the European Union Agency for Railways imply a positive trend of improved safety levels in the Single European Railway Area since 2010. Despite deplorable large accidents in recent years, the number of significant accidents has dropped from 2230 in 2010 to 1565 in 2023. A similar downward trend can be observed for the number of victims of accidents (fatalities and seriously injured). Moreover, most of the reported accidents refer to accidents caused by third parties: road users at level crossings or unauthorised persons trespassing railway tracks. These two categories of accidents account also for 97,4% of all fatalities1. Finally, in respect of military mobility, the Commission promotes the concept of ‘dual-use infrastructure’ to ensure that military mobility projects will positively contribute to the development of the EU rail system and thus society as a whole. The cost reductions advocated by the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) European Coordinator’s report2 are supposed to lower the cost of ERTMS deployment on trains and therefore allow for a wider roll-out of this important safety system.
1 Safety Overview 2025, EU Agency for Railways, March 2025, see figures 2, 8 and 10. Document available at:

https://www.era.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-03/safety-overview-2025.pdf. 2 Work plan of the European coordinator Matthias Ruete, Publications Office of the European Union, 2026, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2832/9894936.
